  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Large Language Models (LLMs), despite extensive pretraining on broad internet corpora, often
struggle to adapt effectively to specialized domains.
There is growing interest in fine-tuning these models for such domains; however, progress is constrained by the scarcity and limited coverage of high-quality, task-relevant data. To address this, synthetic data generation methods such as paraphrasing or knowledge extraction are commonly applied. Although these approaches excel at factual recall and conceptual knowledge, they suffer from two critical shortcomings: (i) they provide minimal support for interpretive reasoning capabilities in these specialized domains, and (ii) they often produce synthetic corpora that are excessively large and redundant, resulting in poor sample efficiency.
To overcome these gaps, we propose an adversarial question-generation framework that produces a compact set of semantically challenging questions. These questions are constructed by comparing the outputs of the model to be adapted and a robust expert model grounded in reference documents, using an iterative, feedback-driven process designed to reveal and address comprehension gaps. Evaluation on specialized subsets of the LegalBench corpus demonstrates that our method achieves greater accuracy with substantially fewer synthetic samples.</p>
  
</div>
<div class="ltx_keywords">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_keywords">Keywords: </h6>Machine Learning, ICML
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Large Language Models (LLMs) pretrained on extensive internet-scale corpora have demonstrated remarkable general-purpose capabilities but often struggle to efficiently adapt to highly specialized, domain-specific knowledge contained within small, focused document sets. This difficulty arises primarily from the models’ unfamiliarity with critical domain-specific facts—which may appear only sparsely or even just once within a limited corpus—making it especially challenging to interpret and integrate these facts through complex reasoning. Although there is growing interest in fine-tuning LLMs for specific domains, progress has been limited due to the scarcity of specialized data, motivating the development of targeted synthetic augmentation approaches.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Recent approaches, such as EntiGraph <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2024b</a>)</cite> and Knowledge-Instruct <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ovadia et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, aim to close the data-efficiency gap by generating synthetic training data from small corpora, typically through structured entity and fact extraction. These methods commonly leverage a large, general-purpose model to generate new training data grounded in the specialized domain documents, which is then used to improve a smaller, domain-specialized model, often via fine-tuning or distillation. While EntiGraph focuses on expanding entity-centric knowledge graphs for continued pretraining, Knowledge-Instruct reformulates extracted knowledge into instruction-response pairs for supervised fine-tuning.
Although these approaches achieve strong performance on tasks focused primarily on factual recall, their effectiveness may diminish when faced with broader comprehension tasks, especially those requiring nuanced interpretation, inference, and integration of complex domain-specific knowledge.
For example, determining insurance coverage for an uncommon event, such as a client experiencing an accident while hiking abroad, requires interpreting rarely encountered or implicitly defined conditions within policy clauses. Resolving such questions involves not merely recalling explicit facts, but understanding nuanced language, subtle contextual implications, and layered dependencies within domain-specific documentation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">This observation suggests that it is not just the quantity of data that matters, but rather the quality and specificity of the augmentation strategies employed, particularly approaches explicitly designed to pinpoint and address specific model deficiencies. Existing augmentation methods generally generate synthetic data indiscriminately or based on pre-defined heuristics, without directly probing which concepts or reasoning tasks are most difficult for the model. This can lead to inefficient training, as much of the augmented data might reinforce knowledge the model already possesses. To address this, an adversarial approach naturally emerges as a promising alternative: by actively generating challenging questions tailored to expose precisely those aspects of reasoning and comprehension where the model exhibits weaknesses.
In this manner, the model is exposed not only to questions that require factual recall but also, and more importantly, to those that demand interpretive and integrative reasoning.
Inspired by principles from active learning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xu et al., 2013</a>)</cite>, boosting <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Freund and Schapire, 1997</a>)</cite>, and distributionally robust optimization (DRO) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Duchi and Namkoong, 2018</a>; <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sinha et al., 2018</a>)</cite>—which enhance learning by focusing on uncertain, misclassified, or worst-case instances where the model may perform poorly—we introduce an adversarial learning framework for smaller domain-specific LLMs. This framework iteratively generates questions, using feedback from a robust expert model, to systematically uncover and address interpretative weaknesses.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We demonstrate our adversarial feedback-driven methodology on specialized legal documents within the LegalBench corpus <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Guha et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, showing how these targeted synthetic datasets substantially improve the domain-specific reasoning capabilities of smaller LLMs. Our method enables these models to achieve performance competitive with much larger counterparts, surpassing entity-centric and instruction-based strategies by more effectively addressing a wider range of nuanced comprehension challenges.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Related Work</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Transfer Learning Across Domains.</span>
A core challenge in natural language processing is adapting language models to new domains where direct supervision or labeled data is scarce. Traditional approaches for cross-domain transfer learning often involve continued pretraining on domain corpora <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gururangan et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Devlin et al., 2019</a>)</cite>, domain-adaptive fine-tuning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Howard and Ruder, 2018</a>; <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lee et al., 2020</a>)</cite>, or leveraging multi-task learning frameworks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ruder, 2017</a>)</cite>. Such methods aim to bridge the gap between general pretraining and the specific terminology, knowledge, or reasoning patterns required in target domains. However, their effectiveness may be constrained by the limited availability of high-quality domain-specific data, motivating the development of more data-efficient adaptation strategies.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Model Distillation and Student-Teacher Paradigms.</span>
To further enhance transfer across domains, model distillation methods have been widely employed <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lin et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sanh et al., 2019</a>)</cite>. In this setup, a large, general-purpose teacher model transfers knowledge to a smaller, specialized student model, typically by having the student mimic the outputs or intermediary representations of the teacher. Recent work has explored domain-adaptive distillation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Turc et al., 2019</a>; <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jiao et al., 2020</a>)</cite>, where the teacher is either fine-tuned or prompted for domain-specific tasks, and the resulting guidance is used to supervise smaller models with reduced resources. These teacher-student setups are related to our approach, but in our case, the teacher model is grounded in the same domain documents as the student. This ensures the feedback is tailored to the specific context, making the supervision more relevant and effective.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Synthetic Data Generation.</span>
Recent approaches adapt language models to specialized domains with limited data by generating synthetic corpora. Entity-centric methods such as EntiGraph <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2024b</a>)</cite> expand on entities and relations via knowledge graphs, while paraphrase-based techniques <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Maini et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ovadia et al., 2024</a>)</cite> diversify training data by rewording existing texts. Instruction-driven approaches like Knowledge-Instruct <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ovadia et al., 2025</a>)</cite> convert extracted domain facts into instruction–response pairs, supporting efficient adaptation under low-resource settings. By contrast, our adversarial, feedback-driven framework improves sample efficiency and reasoning ability by selectively generating questions that require not only factual recall but also deeper context-dependent reasoning.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Alongside these developments, there is increasing interest in using LLMs in iterative feedback loops to refine prompts and tasks. Such feedback-driven frameworks, where the model provides critiques or guidance, underlie our approach.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Prompt Optimization via LLM Feedback.</span>
Recent approaches optimize prompts and inputs using automated feedback generated by large language models.
In these frameworks, prompt refinement are guided by structured critiques or optimization signals
from external LLMs. For instance, methods such as TextGrad <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yüksekgönül et al., 2024</a>)</cite> implement differentiable prompting, iteratively refining queries to maximize a model-evaluated reward. Other techniques leverage LLM feedback loops for instruction tuning and robust evaluation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2024a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Madaan et al., 2023</a>)</cite>. Our adversarial
question generation pipeline builds upon this line of work, using LLM-driven feedback to provide fine-grained, diagnostic supervision in an adversarial optimization framework.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Methodology</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our objective is to enhance both the <span id="S3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">domain-specific knowledge</span>—the understanding and recall of concepts, facts, and language unique to a given specialized corpus—and the <span id="S3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">interpretive reasoning capabilities</span>—that is, the ability to accurately integrate, infer, and reason over such content—of language models, based solely on access to
a domain document <math id="S3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>C</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math>
(e.g., a legal contract). As in prior work, we operate solely with the domain corpus itself, without requiring annotated datasets or downstream task supervision.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To systematically address both types of weaknesses, our approach introduces an iterative adversarial process that generates questions <math id="S3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Q^{(t)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>Q</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q^{(t)}</annotation></semantics></math> targeting the model’s factual gaps and interpretative limitations. For example, some questions may focus on domain-specific terminology, concepts, or facts explicitly present in <math id="S3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>C</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math> (e.g., “What is the definition of the term ‘subrogation’ in this contract?”), while others may present challenging or hypothetical scenarios that require reasoning, inference, or integration of multiple clauses (e.g., “If a client is injured while hiking abroad, would they be covered under this insurance policy?”). A model may, for instance, accurately define ’subrogation’ but fail when asked to determine coverage in a scenario requiring integration of multiple clauses; an adversarial question targeting this scenario reveals such interpretive limitations. In this context, the effectiveness of adversarial question generation may be conceptually likened to pedagogical practices in active learning: rather than solely requiring the passive recall of explicitly stated definitions and isolated facts—analogous to students memorizing material for traditional written exams—comprehensive understanding is better gauged by posing challenging, integrated, or hypothetical scenarios akin to those one might encounter in rigorous oral examinations.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In our setting, we assume access to a large, highly capable language model which, when provided with the full domain corpus <math id="S3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>C</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math> as context, can function as a robust “oracle” or expert. However, relying on such a system—in which the model always has access to all domain documents—is often impractical in real-world scenarios due to resource, latency, privacy, or deployment constraints. Therefore, our aim is to transfer domain expertise from this strong oracle model to a more lightweight, efficient target model.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Adversarial Question Optimization</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We propose an adversarial optimization framework to systematically uncover and address interpretive deficiencies in domain-specific language models. This setup comprises two primary agents: a robust expert model (<math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{\text{strong}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>f</mi><mtext>strong</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{\text{strong}}</annotation></semantics></math>) and a target weaker model (<math id="S3.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{\text{weak}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>f</mi><mtext>weak</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{\text{weak}}</annotation></semantics></math>), both provided with access to the same domain-specific context <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>C</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math>. The core objective is to generate and iteratively refine questions about <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>C</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math> that maximize divergence between the responses of these models, thereby identifying aspects in which the target model exhibits limitations in either domain-specific knowledge or interpretive reasoning.
Formally, at each iteration <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>, we take the domain-specific context or document <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>C</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math> and the current question <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Q_{i}^{(t)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>Q</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q_{i}^{(t)}</annotation></semantics></math>, and obtain answers from both models:</p>
<table id="S3.Ex1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{i,\text{strong}}^{(t)}=f_{\text{strong}}(C,Q_{i}^{(t)}),\quad A_{i,\text{weak}}^{(t)}=f_{\text{weak}}(C,Q_{i}^{(t)})." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext>strong</mtext></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mtext>strong</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>Q</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext>weak</mtext></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mtext>weak</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>Q</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{i,\text{strong}}^{(t)}=f_{\text{strong}}(C,Q_{i}^{(t)}),\quad A_{i,\text{weak}}^{(t)}=f_{\text{weak}}(C,Q_{i}^{(t)}).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We then evaluate the difference in their answers using a feedback function <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{\text{fb}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>f</mi><mtext>fb</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{\text{fb}}</annotation></semantics></math>, which is typically instantiated as a capable LLM to compare the two responses and identify discrepancies along dimensions such as correctness, coverage, and contextual reasoning alignment (see Appendix <a href="#A1.SS3.SSS3" title="A.3.3 Prompt Templates ‣ A.3 Implementation Details ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Agentic Adversarial QA for Improving Domain-Specific LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.3.3</span></a>):</p>
<table id="S3.Ex2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}(Q_{i}^{(t)})=f_{\text{fb}}(A_{i,\text{strong}}^{(t)},A_{i,\text{weak}}^{(t)})." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>Q</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mtext>fb</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext>strong</mtext></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext>weak</mtext></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}(Q_{i}^{(t)})=f_{\text{fb}}(A_{i,\text{strong}}^{(t)},A_{i,\text{weak}}^{(t)}).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.2" class="ltx_p">The key objective of this adversarial process is to generate questions that maximize the measured disagreement, as quantified by <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}(Q)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>Q</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}(Q)</annotation></semantics></math>, which serves as a proxy loss function indicating where the target model most strongly diverges from the expert’s interpretive capacity. Specifically, we seek</p>
<table id="S3.Ex3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Q^{*}=\arg\max_{Q}\mathcal{L}(Q)." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>Q</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>arg</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mrow><munder><mi>max</mi><mi>Q</mi></munder><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>Q</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q^{*}=\arg\max_{Q}\mathcal{L}(Q).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.3" class="ltx_p">To operationalize this iterative maximization over text, we adopt the differentiable prompting paradigm introduced in TextGrad <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yüksekgönül et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. Notably, while TextGrad is designed to minimize a task loss by refining prompts, our framework inverts this direction and explicitly maximizes interpretive disagreement in order to expose the limitations of the target model:</p>
<table id="S3.Ex4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Q_{i}^{(t+1)}=Q_{i}^{(t)}+\nabla_{Q}\mathcal{L}(Q_{i}^{(t)})." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>Q</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>Q</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>+</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><mi>Q</mi></msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>Q</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q_{i}^{(t+1)}=Q_{i}^{(t)}+\nabla_{Q}\mathcal{L}(Q_{i}^{(t)}).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.4" class="ltx_p">Each refinement step comprises two stages: (i) a guidance model (<math id="S3.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{\text{guide}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>f</mi><mtext>guide</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{\text{guide}}</annotation></semantics></math>) generates a natural language editing instruction, conditioned on the output of the feedback model (<math id="S3.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{\text{fb}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>f</mi><mtext>fb</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{\text{fb}}</annotation></semantics></math>): <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nabla_{Q}\mathcal{L}(Q_{i}^{(t)})=f_{\text{guide}}(Q_{i}^{(t)},\mathcal{L}(Q_{i}^{(t)}))" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mo>∇</mo><mi>Q</mi></msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>Q</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mtext>guide</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>Q</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>Q</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nabla_{Q}\mathcal{L}(Q_{i}^{(t)})=f_{\text{guide}}(Q_{i}^{(t)},\mathcal{L}(Q_{i}^{(t)}))</annotation></semantics></math>. This instruction prescribes how to revise <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Q_{i}^{(t)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>Q</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q_{i}^{(t)}</annotation></semantics></math> to accentuate potential weaknesses and failure modes in the target model (see Appendix <a href="#A1.SS3.SSS3" title="A.3.3 Prompt Templates ‣ A.3 Implementation Details ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Agentic Adversarial QA for Improving Domain-Specific LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.3.3</span></a> for examples). (ii) a revision model (<math id="S3.SS1.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{\text{rev}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>f</mi><mtext>rev</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{\text{rev}}</annotation></semantics></math>) applies this instruction to update the current question, yielding the next iteration, <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Q_{i}^{(t+1)}=f_{\text{rev}}(Q_{i}^{(t)},\nabla_{Q}\mathcal{L}(Q_{i}^{(t)}))" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>Q</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mtext>rev</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>Q</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><mi>Q</mi></msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>Q</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q_{i}^{(t+1)}=f_{\text{rev}}(Q_{i}^{(t)},\nabla_{Q}\mathcal{L}(Q_{i}^{(t)}))</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In practice, we instantiate the three auxiliary agents—<math id="S3.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{\text{fb}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>f</mi><mtext>fb</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{\text{fb}}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{\text{guide}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>f</mi><mtext>guide</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{\text{guide}}</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{\text{rev}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>f</mi><mtext>rev</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{\text{rev}}</annotation></semantics></math>—using the same strong LLM, each configured with a distinct instruction prompt (see Appendix <a href="#A1.SS3.SSS3" title="A.3.3 Prompt Templates ‣ A.3 Implementation Details ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Agentic Adversarial QA for Improving Domain-Specific LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.3.3</span></a>). This design preserves semantic consistency across modules while remaining implementation-lightweight. Notably, <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{\text{guide}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>f</mi><mtext>guide</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{\text{guide}}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{\text{rev}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>f</mi><mtext>rev</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{\text{rev}}</annotation></semantics></math> correspond to the <span id="S3.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">TextGrad.backward</span> and <span id="S3.SS1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">TextGrad.step</span> modules, respectively.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Algorithm <a href="#alg1" title="Algorithm 1 ‣ 3.2 Synthetic Dataset Construction and Fine-Tuning ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ Agentic Adversarial QA for Improving Domain-Specific LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> summarizes the entire adversarial question optimization procedure, clearly delineating each step involved in refining questions to systematically identify and improve the interpretive limitations of the target model.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Synthetic Dataset Construction and Fine-Tuning</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">After completing the optimization procedure, we assemble a synthetic dataset consisting of the final adversarial questions paired with expert-provided answers:</p>
<table id="S3.Ex5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}_{\text{synthetic}}=\left\{\left(Q_{i}^{(T)},f_{\text{strong}}(C,Q_{i}^{(T)})\right)\right\}_{i=1}^{N}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>synthetic</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msubsup><mi>Q</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>T</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mtext>strong</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>Q</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>T</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></msubsup></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}_{\text{synthetic}}=\left\{\left(Q_{i}^{(T)},f_{\text{strong}}(C,Q_{i}^{(T)})\right)\right\}_{i=1}^{N}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">Fine-tuning the weak model <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{\text{weak}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>f</mi><mtext>weak</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{\text{weak}}</annotation></semantics></math> on the expert-curated <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}_{\text{synthetic}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>synthetic</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}_{\text{synthetic}}</annotation></semantics></math> explicitly targets and remedies the shortcomings uncovered by adversarial optimization. Consequently, this focused training substantially enhances the model’s robustness and accuracy on domain-specific comprehension tasks.</p>
</div>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_float"><span id="alg1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Algorithm 1</span> </span> Iterative Adversarial Question Generation</figcaption>

initial question set <math id="alg1.l1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{Q_{i}^{(0)}\}_{i=1}^{N}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msubsup><mi>Q</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{Q_{i}^{(0)}\}_{i=1}^{N}</annotation></semantics></math>; <div id="alg1.l6" class="ltx_listingline">

</div>
<div id="alg1.l7" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l7.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">7:</span></span>
              
              
               <math id="alg1.l7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nabla_{Q}\mathcal{L}(Q_{i}^{(t)})\leftarrow f_{\text{guide}}(Q_{i}^{(t)},\,\mathcal{L}(Q_{i}^{(t)}))" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mo>∇</mo><mi>Q</mi></msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>Q</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mtext>guide</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>Q</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>Q</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nabla_{Q}\mathcal{L}(Q_{i}^{(t)})\leftarrow f_{\text{guide}}(Q_{i}^{(t)},\,\mathcal{L}(Q_{i}^{(t)}))</annotation></semantics></math>

</div>
<div id="alg1.l8" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l8.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">8:</span></span>
              
              
               <math id="alg1.l8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Q_{i}^{(t+1)}\leftarrow f_{\text{rev}}(Q_{i}^{(t)},\,\nabla_{Q}\mathcal{L}(Q_{i}^{(t)}))" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>Q</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mtext>rev</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>Q</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><mi>Q</mi></msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>Q</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q_{i}^{(t+1)}\leftarrow f_{\text{rev}}(Q_{i}^{(t)},\,\nabla_{Q}\mathcal{L}(Q_{i}^{(t)}))</annotation></semantics></math>

</div>

              <span id="alg1.l9.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">end</span> <span id="alg1.l9.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">for</span>
</div>
<div id="alg1.l10" class="ltx_listingline">

             <span id="alg1.l11.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Return:</span> <math id="alg1.l11.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{Q_{i}^{(T)}\}_{i=1}^{N}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msubsup><mi>Q</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>T</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{Q_{i}^{(T)}\}_{i=1}^{N}</annotation></semantics></math> <span id="alg1.l11.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">(Final set of optimized questions)</span>

</div>

</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Experiments</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We assess our method on a targeted subset of the <span id="S4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">LegalBench</span> benchmark <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Guha et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, which originally comprises a wide range of tasks intended to evaluate the legal reasoning abilities of large language models. To emphasize domain-specific abilities, we focus on the three most frequently referenced contracts from the CUAD dataset <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hendrycks et al., 2021</a>)</cite> within the LegalBench suite. These are: <span id="S4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Cardlytics Maintenance Agreement</span>, <span id="S4.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Buffalo Wild Wings Franchise Agreement</span>, and <span id="S4.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">PF Hospitality Franchise Agreement</span>. Across these contracts, there are a total of 491 benchmark questions spanning 36 distinct tasks.</p>
</div>

</table>
</figure>
<div id="S4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We compare our proposed fine-tuning approach against a base pretrained LLM , as well as several increasingly sophisticated domain adaptation strategies. These include (1) paraphrase-based fine-tuning; (2) fine-tuning on uninformed questions, a naive synthetic dataset generated by prompting a strong LLM to write challenging questions for a given contract without any iterative refinement or adversarial objective; (3) EntiGraph-based augmentation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2024b</a>)</cite>; and (4) Knowledge-Instruct <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ovadia et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
All models are evaluated using a few-shot setting with the standard LegalBench prompt template. To isolate the effects of fine-tuning strategies, we do not employ any retrieval augmentation or external tools.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Our adversarial QA generation approach consistently outperforms both paraphrase-based fine-tuning and model-independent questions fine-tuning baselines. It achieves a <span id="S4.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">18.99%</span> improvement over the base model and a <span id="S4.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">3.89%</span> gain relative to the EntiGraph competitor, while using <math id="S4.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\approx" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>≈</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\approx</annotation></semantics></math>70<math id="S4.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> fewer training tokens. Whereas EntiGraph primarily augments entity-level relational knowledge, our feedback-driven question optimization specifically targets interpretive shortcomings, leading to richer semantic coverage and greater task accuracy.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p4.1" class="ltx_p">To assess the impact of iterative adversarial refinement, we perform a sensitivity analysis by varying the number of optimization steps during dataset construction. For each contract, we generate adversarial questions with different refinement iterations, fine-tune the target model, and evaluate on the corresponding LegalBench tasks.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F1" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18137v1/adversarial_qa_optimization_epochs.svg" id="S4.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/278;" width="476" height="278"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span>
Accuracy on LegalBench (top three contracts) by epoch; performance improves with more refinement.
</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p5.1" class="ltx_p">As shown in Figure <a href="#S4.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Agentic Adversarial QA for Improving Domain-Specific LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, additional refinement iterations result in progressively higher accuracy, highlighting the effectiveness of iterative adversarial feedback in improving domain-specific model performance.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We introduce an adversarial question generation framework to enhance domain-specific LLMs by systematically identifying and addressing their interpretive weaknesses. By adapting the TextGrad differentiable prompting method, our approach iteratively produces targeted questions and synthetic datasets aligned with model-specific shortcomings. Empirical results demonstrate that this strategy substantially improves the reasoning performance of smaller LLMs, even in limited data settings, highlighting the effectiveness of adversarial refinement for efficient domain adaptation.</p>
</div>
</section>

</span></li>
